ADHD

A sham-controlled study found improved correct-rejection performance and increased prefrontal oxygenation after one PBM session in adults with ADHD. A separate uncontrolled study reported improved attention and working-memory tests after repeated sessions.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A sham-controlled study found improved correct-rejection performance and increased prefrontal oxygenation after one PBM session in adults with ADHD. A separate uncontrolled study reported improved attention and working-memory tests after repeated sessions.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact ADHD category contains three unique publications: two human studies and one rat experiment. One human publication is a randomized sham-controlled, two-stage study, and the other is a 48-person single-arm study. They test different schedules and cognitive measures, with no reported cohort overlap. The rat experiment uses a spontaneous-hypertension model commonly used to study ADHD-like behavior; it is not a human treatment study.

Human and clinical evidence

In the randomized study, 223 adults with and without a history of ADHD took part in the first stage, and a second stage focused on 52 adults with ADHD. After a single active 1064 nm session, adults in the ADHD subgroup showed a 51% increase in correct rejections on a continuous-performance task compared with sham, reaching performance similar to the non-ADHD group. In the second stage, correct rejections on a working-memory task improved, and near-infrared spectroscopy showed higher prefrontal oxygenated and total hemoglobin after active treatment. These are acute task and blood-oxygenation findings rather than evidence of symptom control over time (Salehpour et al. 2026).

A separate study treated 48 adults daily for seven days and reported improvements in working memory and attention measures that were still present at a four-week follow-up. Because the study had no control group, practice effects, expectation, and changes over time remain possible explanations alongside PBM (Lai et al. 2025).

Animal evidence

In spontaneously hypertensive rats, daily 808 nm PBM for 21 days reduced open-field distance and movement speed compared with sham, while prefrontal fractional anisotropy increased and Iba-1-positive microglia decreased. The study also reported preservation of myelin in ADHD-related regions. These behavioral and tissue findings come from one rat model and do not establish a human dose or effect (Huang et al. 2025).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No cell or ex-vivo study is classified in the ADHD category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The two adult studies used 1064 nm near-infrared laser light on the right prefrontal area. The randomized study used a single four-minute session at 3.4 W and 0.25 W/cm², corresponding to 60 J/cm². The uncontrolled study used seven daily sessions of about 12 minutes. The rat experiment instead used 808 nm near-infrared light for 25 seconds daily. These protocols do not establish a preferred schedule, and the human studies have not yet tested durable changes in core ADHD symptoms or day-to-day functioning.

Interpretation

The randomized comparison found better short-term impulse-control task performance and increased prefrontal oxygenation after PBM. A separate uncontrolled study reported later cognitive-test improvements, while one rat experiment found behavioral and tissue changes in an ADHD-like model. The next clinical question is whether repeated PBM improves symptoms and functioning beyond cognitive-test performance.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for single-session impulse-control task performance and prefrontal oxygenation Low for sustained attention, core symptoms, and everyday function
Publications and records3 unique publications

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

A sham-controlled adult study found better impulse-control task performance and increased prefrontal oxygenation after one session, with a large task effect in the ADHD subgroup. A separate repeated-session study reported cognitive-test gains but lacked a control group. Replicated trials using repeated treatment and validated symptom and daily-function measures are needed to show whether the acute task result becomes a lasting clinical benefit.
